name: Pseudopolynomial-Regime Algorithms and Proximity for Subset Sum
description: The pseudopolynomial line for Subset Sum studies running times polynomial in the number n of items and in the target t (or the maximum item size), as opposed to the exponential-in-n worst-case regime. Bellman's 1957 DP solves Subset Sum in O(nt); Bringmann (SODA 2017) gave the first randomized O~(n+t) algorithm via two-level color coding and sparse convolution, and Chan (SODA 2026) gave the first deterministic O~(t) algorithm, derandomizing both Bringmann's and the more recent output-sensitive algorithms using (min,+) matrix multiplication. The output-sensitive refinement was driven by Bringmann-Nakos (STOC 2020, O~(|S(X,t)|^{4/3})) and Bringmann-Fischer-Nakos (SODA 2025, O~(|S(X,t)|·sqrt(n))), which beats Bellman in every regime using a new additive-combinatorics sumset estimate. In parallel, proximity techniques (Eisenbrand-Weismantel's Steinitz-lemma proximity theorem and its algorithmic descendants, including small-item algorithms and l0-proximity) bound how far an optimal integer solution can be from a fractional/LP solution, reducing subset-sum-like problems with small items or bounded coefficients to small residual searches. Together these results show that the dense/small-value corner is essentially solved in near-linear time and use conditional lower bounds to delineate exactly where the remaining exponential hardness (and hence any 2^(n/3) target) must live.
worst_case_time: Bellman DP: O(nt) deterministic. Best randomized pseudopolynomial: Bringmann (SODA 2017) O~(n+t). Best deterministic: Chan (SODA 2026) O~(t); previously Koiliaris-Xu (SODA 2017) deterministic O~(t·sqrt(n)). Output-sensitive: Bringmann-Nakos (STOC 2020) O~(|S(X,t)|^{4/3}); Bringmann-Fischer-Nakos (SODA 2025) O~(|S(X,t)|·sqrt(n)), which beats Bellman's O(n|S(X,t)|) in all regimes. Small items: Polak-Rohwedder-Wegrzycki (ICALP 2021) O~(n+s^{5/3}) for Subset Sum (and O(n+s^3) for Knapsack), where s is the maximum item size; l0-proximity gives O~(n+w_max^{1.5}).
space_complexity: Bellman DP: O(t) (a bitset/array over [0,t]). Bringmann's O~(n+t) algorithm is usually implemented in O(t) space [uncertain]. Chan's deterministic O~(t) algorithm is derived from min-plus matrix multiplication and does not change the space asymptotically [uncertain]. Output-sensitive algorithms must at least output S(X,t), so they use Omega(|S(X,t)|) space; exact bounds are not emphasized in BN/BFN. Small-item and proximity-based algorithms use O(n+s)- or O(n+w_max)-style space [uncertain].
model: Classical word RAM / unit-cost RAM with word size O(log(nt)) (needed for FFT-based convolution, bitset DP, and (min,+) matrix multiplication). No quantum model; all results here are classical and deterministic or randomized as noted.
randomized_or_deterministic: Bringmann (SODA 2017), Bringmann-Nakos (STOC 2020) and Bringmann-Fischer-Nakos (SODA 2025) are randomized (Monte Carlo, high probability), using color coding and sparse convolution. Koiliaris-Xu (SODA 2017) and Chan (SODA 2026) are deterministic; Chan's is the first deterministic O~(t). Polak-Rohwedder-Wegrzycki (ICALP 2021) is deterministic for its O~(n+s^{5/3}) Subset Sum bound [uncertain]; the l0-proximity line uses randomization.
time_space_tradeoff_curve: Single points for the pseudopolynomial algorithms above. The broader exact-subset-sum literature has rich time-space tradeoffs (Schroeppel-Shamir T=2^n/S^2, Lokshtanov-Nederlof algebraization, Nederlof-Wegrzycki), but the pseudopolynomial/proximity results are not parameterized by a space budget. Bellman O(nt)/O(t) is the baseline point; output-sensitive algorithms range over the output size |S(X,t)|.
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: No exponential-in-n exponent: complexity is pseudopolynomial (polynomial in n and t). Timeline of constants: Bellman 1957 O(nt); Koiliaris-Xu 2017 deterministic O~(t sqrt n); Bringmann 2017 randomized O~(n+t); Jin-Wu SOSA 2019 simpler randomized O~(n+t); Bringmann-Nakos STOC 2020 O~(|S|^{4/3}); Bringmann-Fischer-Nakos SODA 2025 O~(|S| sqrt n); Chan SODA 2026 deterministic O~(t). These give O(2^{(1/3+o(1))n}) whenever t <= 2^{(1/3+o(1))n}, i.e. they meet the 2^(n/3) target throughout the small-value regime.
problem_variant: Vanilla Subset Sum computing the set S(X,t) of all attainable sums up to t (output-sensitive / counting via generating functions); 0-1 Knapsack; Unbounded Subset Sum; a vector/generalized Subset Sum (BFN extend their ideas); Subset Sum with small items; C-Subset Sum / bounded ILP via proximity.
applies_to: Given n positive integers X and target t, compute or decide the attainable subset sums S(X,t). Bringmann-Fischer-Nakos additionally handle a vector variant and Unbounded Subset Sum. Proximity results apply to bounded ILP, C-Subset Sum with constant coefficient set, and n-fold IP formulations of subset sum.
coefficient_set: C = {0,1} for standard 0-1 Subset Sum; {0,...,c} (bounded variable values) for C-Subset Sum / bounded ILP; {-1,0,1} for Equal Subset Sum. Proximity bounds are stated in terms of the constraint dimension m and the maximum coefficient Delta = max|a_i|; small-item results are stated in terms of s = max a_i.
density_regime: Targets the dense / small-value / small-item regimes: near-linear when t or the maximum item is small or polynomially bounded, output-sensitive in |S(X,t)|, and bounded-coefficient/constant-dimension for the ILP-proximity line. Crucially it does NOT address the low-density (n-bit, large-value) regime d = n/log2(max|a_i|) near or below ~1, which is exactly where the exponential-in-n algorithms (2^(n/2) MITM, 2^(n/3) target) are relevant.
solution_regime: General decision/output of all attainable sums with no promise on the number of solutions; also the counting/output variant. No pigeonhole promise (Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum is a separate promise problem).
cardinality_constraint: No fixed-cardinality/Hamming-layer constraint; standard Subset Sum and Knapsack. (Cardinality-constrained variants are handled elsewhere.)
key_technique: Bellman DP. Bringmann: two-level color coding partitions items so each color class is small enough that its sumset is computed by sparse convolution / FFT, and the class sumsets are combined. Bringmann-Nakos: sparse convolution plus additive-combinatorics sumset estimates (sub-multiplicativity of sumsets) for output-sensitive computation. Bringmann-Fischer-Nakos: color coding + sparse convolution + a new additive-combinatorics estimate that bounds the cost of computing a sumset only inside the target box (without generating the much larger unrestricted sumset). Chan: derandomization using the Chan-Williams deterministic (min,+) matrix multiplication and a deterministic version of the Cygan et al. reduction from 0-1 Knapsack to (min,+) convolution. Proximity: Eisenbrand-Weismantel's Steinitz-lemma proximity theorem bounds the l1-distance between an optimal integer solution and an optimal LP solution; l0-proximity bounds the number of differing coordinates.
core_idea: Pseudopolynomial DP costs O(nt); color coding shrinks each color class enough that its sumset can be computed by FFT and the sumsets combined, yielding O~(n+t) for small t. Additive combinatorics supplies that sumsets cannot grow faster than a controlled function of the number of terms, enabling output-sensitive bounds that beat the O(n|S|) DP whenever the attainable-sum set is sparse. Proximity says an optimal solution differs from a fractional/LP solution in only a few coordinates (l0) or by a small l1 amount, so most items can be fixed and only a small residual instance remains to be searched (small-item DP). Constraint on the 2^(n/3) target: when t <= 2^{(1/3+o(1))n} the pseudopolynomial algorithms already run in O*(2^(n/3)) or faster, so a 2^(n/3) algorithm only adds value in the large-value/low-density regime; and SETH lower bounds rule out naive pseudo-poly x exponential hybrids.
reduction_pipeline: Subset Sum computes S(X,t) directly. Fine-grained reductions: 0-1 Knapsack reduces to (min,+) convolution (Cygan-Mucha-Wegrzycki-Wlodarczyk, ICALP 2017; derandomized by Chan, SODA 2026); C-Subset Sum reduces to bounded ILP / n-fold IP (proximity line); Subset Sum reduces to computing sumsets / sparse convolution. These reductions transfer upper bounds and conditional lower bounds between Subset Sum, Knapsack, (min,+) convolution, and ILP.
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive: the algorithms output the full set S(X,t) (and can return a witness subset). Proximity arguments are constructive in that they bound and locate the residual search; some proximity theorems are existence statements about a close optimal solution that then drive an algorithm.
search_vs_decision_witness: Primarily computes all attainable sums (a superset of deciding feasibility), from which a decision and a witness subset are immediate; some proximity-based methods return only the optimum/witness. Output-sensitive statements refer to listing S(X,t).
obstacle_to_2n3: Pseudopolynomial and proximity methods are polynomial in t (and/or s) and therefore give no O*(2^{(1/2-eps)n}) or O*(2^{n/3}) worst-case bound in the n-bit/low-density regime; they settle the dense/small-value corner, not the hard large-value corner. Precise constraint on a 2^(n/3) algorithm: it must strictly beat these methods exactly when t is large (near 2^n), where O~(t) is about 2^n; in the range t <= 2^{n/3} the pseudopolynomial algorithms already match the target, so a 2^(n/3) result must come from exploiting low-density structure. Moreover SETH-based lower bounds of the form 'no O(t^{1-eps} 2^{delta n})' show that one cannot obtain 2^(n/3) by combining the fastest pseudopolynomial algorithm (O~(t)) with a generic exponential search; and the Cygan et al. reduction to (min,+) convolution ties further progress to subquadratic (min,+) convolution, which is not known and is conjectured impossible.
potential_to_break_mitm: Low directly: these algorithms have polynomial exponent in t and do not change the 2^(n/2) worst-case exponent for large values. High indirectly: they clarify that the only remaining hard regime is large values / low density and provide the additive-combinatorics and proximity toolkit used by output-sensitive and representation/mixing approaches. The 2^(n/3) target, if reachable, must come from the low-density representation line, not from faster pseudopolynomial algorithms.
barrier_evidence: Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay (SODA 2019 / ACM TALG 2022; arXiv:1704.04546) prove, under SETH, that Subset Sum cannot be solved in O(t^{1-eps} 2^{delta n}) time (a pseudo-polynomial x exponential lower bound). Bringmann-Wellnitz (SODA 2021; arXiv:2010.09096) prove the near-linear dense-subset-sum regime is optimal under SETH plus a strong k-SUM hypothesis. Cygan et al. (ICALP 2017) show 0-1 Knapsack is equivalent to (min,+) convolution, so barriers for convolution transfer. Polak-Rohwedder-Wegrzycki derive Min-Plus-Convolution-Conjecture-conditional lower bounds (no O((nt)^{0.99}) / O((st)^{0.99}) Knapsack algorithms). Proximity bounds limit ILP approaches to bounded coefficients/constant dimension.
open_questions: Is deterministic near-linear O~(n+t) time possible (Chan's O~(t) is deterministic but not O~(n+t))? Can the output-size exponent be pushed below 1, e.g. O~(|S(X,t)| n^{1/2-eps})? Can the proximity bound for unbounded-variable / general Subset Sum be improved (optimal proximity bounds)? Does an output-sensitive improvement translate into a better worst-case exponential exponent? How do proximity and additive-combinatorics tools interact with the low-density/high-value regime that governs the 2^(n/3) question?
conditional_hypothesis: SETH (via the Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay pseudo-polynomial lower bounds), the strong k-SUM hypothesis (Bringmann-Wellnitz dense-subset-sum lower bound), the (min,+) convolution conjecture (via the Cygan et al. equivalence), and ETH for the exponential regime. The proximity results themselves are unconditional (Steinitz lemma).
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: Worst-case guarantees: Chan is deterministic O~(t) on every instance; Bringmann/BN/BFN are randomized with high-probability worst-case guarantees. Output-sensitive bounds hold for every instance given its value of |S(X,t)|. Small-item algorithms give worst-case bounds but may use random partitioning inside. Proximity bounds are unconditional and worst-case for bounded ILP. None of these degrade to average-case-only.
cryptographic_regime: Indirect. Low-density (high-value) knapsacks, where lattice attacks operate, are outside the pseudopolynomial regime: DP is exponential in n when t ~ 2^n. Pseudopolynomial algorithms apply to dense/small-item instances and thus do not break lattice-hard knapsacks; the proximity/ILP connection (n-fold IP) has not yielded knapsack-cryptosystem breaks. The pseudo-polynomial lower bounds do constrain the design space for attacks on small-value instances.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: This item is the pseudopolynomial regime itself. The key interaction is hybrid algorithm design: run DP / color-coding / output-sensitive convolution when t or the items are small, and switch to MITM or representation/mixing when values are large. SETH lower bounds formalize that neither technique alone breaks the 2^(n/2) barrier. Proximity (Eisenbrand-Weismantel, l0-proximity, small items) directly connects the bounded-coefficient / small-item regime to bounded ILP and to the cardinality/coefficient-set structure exploited in worst-case representation mixing.

empirical_evidence: None primary. These are theoretical complexity results; no standard benchmark suite is reported in the papers. Bringmann's O~(n+t) and the small-item algorithms are often noted as practically relevant, but no systematic empirical study is presented.
implementation_artifact: none found. The algorithms are theoretical (FFT/sparse-convolution/color-coding and ILP-proximity); no canonical reference repository accompanies the cited papers.
verification_method: Implement Bellman's O(nt) DP and compare on random instances against the claimed near-linear output-sensitive algorithms; verify the color-coding partition and the sumset estimate empirically by measuring sumset growth; reproduce the Cygan et al. (min,+) convolution reduction on small Knapsack instances; for proximity, verify the l1/l0 proximity bound on bounded-ILP instances and confirm the resulting FPT/small-item algorithm's correctness.
uncertain: randomized_or_deterministic (deterministic vs randomized status of the Polak-Rohwedder-Wegrzycki O~(n+s^{5/3}) bound)
